title: Statements & Conclusions
intro: This family — conclusions, assumptions, arguments, courses of action — tests whether something logically rests on the given statement, using ONLY the statement and general knowledge, never your opinions or extra facts. The discipline is to ask a precise question for each type and reject anything that needs information not present.

items.name: Conclusion
items.formula: must necessarily follow from the statement alone

items.name: Assumption
items.formula: something unstated but TAKEN FOR GRANTED

items.name: Argument
items.formula: strong if directly relevant + significant; weak if trivial/irrelevant

items.name: Course of action
items.formula: valid if it actually addresses the problem and is practical

items.name: Rule
items.formula: use only the statement + common knowledge — no personal views

topics.name: Statement & Conclusions
topics.details: A conclusion follows only if it is a logical consequence of the statement — not merely plausible or likely true in the world. Reject conclusions that overstate (add 'all', 'always'), introduce comparisons not given, or require outside facts.

solved.problem: Statement: 'All the trees in the park are tall.' Conclusion: Some tall things are in the park?
solved.solution: The tall trees are in the park, so some tall things are in the park. Follows.

solved.problem: Statement: 'Smoking causes cancer.' Conclusion: One should avoid smoking?
solved.solution: Avoiding a known cause of harm follows reasonably. Follows.

solved.problem: Statement: 'The shop opens at 9 am.' Conclusion: The shop is closed before 9 am?
solved.solution: Opening at 9 implies it is not open before 9. Follows.

solved.problem: Statement: 'Many students passed the exam.' Conclusion: All students passed?
solved.solution: "Many" does not mean "all". Does not follow.

unsolved.problem: Statement: 'It rained heavily, so the match was cancelled.' Conclusion: Rain can affect matches?
Statement: 'Some books are interesting.' Conclusion: All books are interesting?
Statement: 'The bridge is closed for repairs.' Conclusion: The bridge is currently unusable?
Statement: 'He scored more than 90%.' Conclusion: He is the topper?
Statement: 'All metals expand on heating.' Conclusion: Iron expands on heating?

topics.name: Statement & Assumptions
topics.details: An assumption is something the speaker takes for granted — without it the statement makes no sense. Test by negation: if denying the assumption breaks the statement, it is assumed. Reject far-fetched or merely possible assumptions.

solved.problem: Statement: 'Please switch off your phone during the film.' Assumption: Phones can disturb others?
solved.solution: The request only makes sense if phones can disturb. Assumed.

solved.problem: Statement: 'Buy our soap for soft skin.' Assumption: People want soft skin?
solved.solution: The pitch presumes the desire exists. Assumed.

solved.problem: Statement: 'Take an umbrella; it may rain.' Assumption: An umbrella helps against rain?
solved.solution: The advice relies on it. Assumed.

solved.problem: Statement: 'The notice is in English.' Assumption: Everyone knows English?
solved.solution: Far-fetched/over-general — not necessarily assumed. Not assumed.

unsolved.problem: Statement: 'Use the stairs during a fire.' Assumption: Lifts are unsafe in a fire?
Statement: 'Apply before 5 pm.' Assumption: Applications close at 5 pm?
Statement: 'Our course guarantees success.' Assumption: The course is the only path to success?
Statement: 'Wear a helmet while riding.' Assumption: Helmets improve safety?
Statement: 'Read the manual before use.' Assumption: The manual has useful information?

topics.name: Statement & Arguments
topics.details: An argument is strong if it is directly relevant and addresses a significant aspect; weak if trivial, irrelevant, an over-generalisation, or based on a questionable assumption. Judge relevance and weight, not whether you agree.

solved.problem: Should plastic bags be banned? Argument: Yes, they cause serious pollution.
Should plastic bags be banned? Argument: No, my shopkeeper likes them.
Should exams be abolished? Argument: Yes, because students dislike them.
solved.solution: Disliking is not a sound basis. Weak.

solved.problem: Should cycling be promoted in cities? Argument: Yes, it reduces traffic and pollution.

unsolved.problem: Should smoking be banned in public? Argument: Yes, it harms non-smokers.
Should homework be stopped? Argument: No, because it has always existed.
Should public transport be free? Argument: Yes, it helps low-income commuters.
Should TV be banned? Argument: No, because some shows are bad.
Should helmets be compulsory? Argument: Yes, they cut head injuries.

topics.name: Course of Action
topics.details: A course of action is a practical step to solve a stated problem. It is valid if it directly addresses the problem and is feasible. Reject actions that are extreme, impractical, or that ignore the actual problem.

solved.problem: Problem: A road has frequent accidents. Action: Install speed breakers and signs?
Problem: Students fail a subject. Action: Hold extra classes?
Problem: A city faces water shortage. Action: Ban all industries permanently?
Problem: A shop loses customers. Action: Improve service and prices?

unsolved.problem: Problem: Frequent power cuts. Action: Upgrade the local grid?
Problem: A river is polluted. Action: Close the whole city?
Problem: Exam cheating rises. Action: Increase invigilation?
Problem: A bus is always late. Action: Review and fix the schedule?
Problem: Litter in a park. Action: Add bins and fines?

shortcuts: Use only the statement + common knowledge — never personal opinion or extra facts.
Conclusion: must NECESSARILY follow; reject over-strong wording (all/always).
Assumption: test by negation — if denying it breaks the statement, it is assumed.
Argument: strong = relevant + significant; weak = trivial/irrelevant.
Course of action: must directly address the problem AND be practical.
mistakes: Marking a conclusion "follows" because it is true in real life, not from the statement.
Judging arguments by agreement rather than relevance/weight.
Approving extreme or impractical courses of action.
pyq: SSC mixes conclusion and assumption items in Tier 1; arguments and course-of-action appear in Tier 2. The negation test for assumptions is the single most useful tool.

flashcards.a: It necessarily follows from the statement
Negate it — does the statement break?

summary: Decide each item from the statement alone plus general knowledge. Conclusions must necessarily follow; assumptions are what the statement takes for granted (negation test); arguments are judged on relevance and weight; courses of action must directly and practically address the problem. Reject anything over-strong, trivial, or needing outside facts.
